contentMarkdown:
# Atomic Design

Atomic Design is Brad Frost’s method for thinking about interfaces through five connected stages: atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages. It helps teams work with reusable pieces while checking how those pieces behave in a complete interface.

## What do the five stages mean?

| Stage | Flight-search example |
|---|---|
| Atoms | A label, input, and button. |
| Molecules | A labeled destination field with supporting text. |
| Organisms | A search form combining route, dates, travelers, and actions. |
| Templates | The structural arrangement of search, results, and supporting content. |
| Pages | That arrangement populated with actual content and states. |

The stages support thinking across levels of detail. Teams can move between the search form and a populated results page as they learn what the interface requires.

## How does Atomic Design help in practice?

A team can reuse a destination field while examining how it fits inside different search forms. The populated page exposes constraints that isolated components may miss, such as long airport names, a missing date, or an empty result set.

Use the method alongside component APIs, accessibility requirements, tokens, and maintenance decisions. Define names and boundaries that your team can understand, and review real product states before deciding that a reusable piece is complete.

## Related terms

- [Design Primitives](/glossary/design-primitives.html)
- [Component Libraries](/glossary/component-libraries.html)
- [Design System](/glossary/design-system.html)

sources: Overview of variables, collections, and modes, Figma (https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/14506821864087-Overview-of-variables-collections-and-modes)
contentMarkdown:
# Figma Variables & Modes

Figma variables store reusable values that you can apply to supported design properties. A collection groups variables, and its modes provide different sets of values for those variables. Switching a frame’s mode changes how its bound properties resolve, so the same design can show a light or dark theme.

## How do variables, collections, and modes work?

Figma supports color, number, string, and Boolean variables. A variable can store a value directly or reference another variable through an alias. A collection defines which modes its variables share. Each mode supplies one value per variable.

| In Figma | Example |
|---|---|
| Palette collection | Color variables named `blue/600` and `blue/300` |
| Semantic colors collection | Light and Dark modes |
| Semantic variable | `color/text/link`, referencing `blue/600` in Light and `blue/300` in Dark |

Bind the link’s text fill to the semantic variable. In the frame’s Appearance settings, choose Light or Dark for the Semantic colors collection. The same link layer keeps its variable binding as the color changes. Check contrast against the actual background in both themes.

## Why is a layer still showing the wrong mode?

For a collection, an object set to Auto looks up its parent hierarchy for an explicit mode. If a nested frame has an explicit override, its children can use that mode even when the outer frame changes. Check the layer’s binding, the collection it comes from, and the nearest mode setting. When no override applies, Figma uses the applicable default.

Use separate collections for choices that need to vary independently. A color theme and a spacing density can have separate modes so you can review Dark with either Compact or Comfortable spacing.

## Can you use Figma variables as design tokens?

Variables can represent token decisions inside Figma. Figma documents DTCG JSON import for supported token types and JSON export of variable modes. For example, its dimension import expects pixels, and its duration import expects seconds. Cross-collection alias import uses Figma-specific extension data.

Try exporting Light and Dark and importing them into a test collection. Check both values and whether the link variable still references its palette variable. If Figma cannot find the target collection, check the mapping before using the files in a [design-to-code workflow](/glossary/design-to-code-workflow.html). Agree on which source owns the values and how a change reaches the application.

## Related terms

- [Semantic Tokens](/glossary/semantic-tokens.html)
- [Design Tokens](/glossary/design-tokens.html)
- [Design-to-Code Workflow](/glossary/design-to-code-workflow.html)
- [Design Tokens Format Module (DTCG)](/glossary/design-tokens-format-module-dtcg.html)

- [Theming](/glossary/design-system-theming.html)

name: Semantic HTML
definition: Semantic HTML means choosing HTML elements that describe the purpose of content and controls. Elements such as headings, links, buttons, and form labels give browsers information about a page’s structure and how people can interact with it.
sources: AI Features and Your Website, Google Search Central (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)
contentMarkdown:
# Semantic HTML

Semantic HTML means choosing HTML elements that describe the purpose of content and controls. Elements such as headings, links, buttons, and form labels give browsers information about a page’s structure and how people can interact with it.

## How does semantic HTML support accessibility?

A browser uses HTML semantics to expose information such as roles, names, and states through its accessibility tree. A screen reader can use that information to identify a button or navigate by headings. An `<a href>` is a link to a destination. A native `<button>` is a control for an action and provides keyboard focus and activation by default. A generic `<div>` with a click handler needs extra work to provide comparable behavior.

## Example: A quote request

```html
<form action="/quote" method="post">
  <label for="quote-email">Email address</label>
  <input id="quote-email" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Request a quote</button>
</form>
```

The label names the field, and the button text describes what happens next. In a real flow, test whether users can recover from validation errors and perceive the submission confirmation.

## How does this help AI browser agents?

Some browser agents use the accessibility tree to inspect a page. The WebArena benchmark, for example, records accessibility-tree observations alongside the agent’s actions. An agent using that view can look for an email field and a “Request a quote” button. Other agents may inspect the DOM or work from screenshots, so test the full task with the agent you care about.

Search discovery is a separate issue. For Google Search’s AI features, a supporting page must be indexed and eligible to appear with a snippet. Google requires no special markup for these features, and it selects supporting pages separately for each response.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)](/glossary/aria-accessible-rich-internet-applications.html)
- [Web Components](/glossary/web-components.html)
- [Structured Data for LLMs](/glossary/structured-data-for-llms.html)

## Sources

- [Sections, WHATWG HTML Living Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html)
- [Forms, WHATWG HTML Living Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html)

contentMarkdown:
# Accessibility and WCAG

Web accessibility means designing and building websites and tools that people with disabilities can use. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), developed through the W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, provide testable requirements for making web content more accessible.

Accessibility addresses visual, auditory, motor, cognitive, and other access needs. WCAG provides a technical baseline; usability testing with people with disabilities helps teams understand barriers in real tasks.

## What are the four WCAG principles?

WCAG organizes its requirements under four principles, often abbreviated **POUR**:

| Principle | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| Perceivable | Provide information people can perceive, such as [alt text](/glossary/alt-text.html) for meaningful images and captions for video. |
| Operable | Make controls usable with different input methods, including a keyboard. |
| Understandable | Use clear instructions, predictable behavior, and helpful error messages. |
| Robust | Expose content and controls so browsers and assistive technologies can interpret them. |

## What do A, AA, and AAA mean?

These are cumulative conformance levels. **A** covers Level A criteria. **AA** includes A and AA. **AAA** includes all three levels. A conformance claim records the version, level, scope, date, and technologies relied upon. Conformance applies to full pages. When a page is part of a process, such as checkout, every step in that process must conform at the claimed level.

## How do WCAG 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2 differ?

| Version | What it adds or establishes |
|---|---|
| **WCAG 2.0** | The original WCAG 2 baseline, covering areas such as text alternatives, keyboard access, and text contrast. |
| **WCAG 2.1** | Adds criteria for mobile use, low vision, and other access needs, including reflow, non-text contrast, and status messages. |
| **WCAG 2.2** | Adds criteria for focus obscured by overlapping content, minimum pointer target size, alternatives to dragging, and accessible authentication, among others. It removes criterion 4.1.1 Parsing. |

WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation. WCAG 3 remains a working draft. Record the WCAG version your team targets and the version required by any applicable regulation or contract. If you report against WCAG 2.0 or 2.1, account for their published treatment of 4.1.1 and any reporting requirements.

## How does WCAG relate to accessibility requirements in the EU and U.S.?

Start with the organization, service, and market. Then identify the applicable rule or contract and the technical version it references.

| Product or organization | Where to start |
|---|---|
| Consumer e-commerce or another covered service in the EU | [European Accessibility Act](/glossary/european-accessibility-act.html) and the applicable national law. |
| An EU public sector website or mobile app | The Web Accessibility Directive and its referenced edition of [EN 301 549](/glossary/en-301-549.html). |
| A U.S. state or local government, or a U.S. business covered by the ADA | [ADA Web Accessibility](/glossary/ada-web-accessibility.html). The Title II web rule references WCAG 2.1 AA. Review Title III separately for covered businesses. |
| ICT developed, used, or procured by a U.S. federal agency | [Section 508](/glossary/section-508.html) and the applicable federal ICT requirements. |

## Which WCAG 2.2 checks matter in everyday design?

These examples are a starting point, not a complete audit:

- **Text contrast, 1.4.3 (AA):** Most text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large-scale text needs 3:1: at least 18 pt, or 14 pt bold. The criterion includes exceptions, such as logos and inactive controls. See [WCAG Color Contrast](/glossary/wcag-color-contrast.html) for control colors and examples across themes. [Contrast (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html)
- **Target size, 2.5.8 (AA):** Pointer targets must be at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels unless an exception applies. See [Touch Target Size](/glossary/touch-target-size.html) for the spacing test and a table example. [Target Size (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)
- **Focus visibility:** Keyboard focus must be visible under 2.4.7 (AA). Under 2.4.11 (AA), a focused component must not be entirely hidden by author-created content, such as a sticky banner. The separate Focus Appearance criterion, 2.4.13, is AAA. See [Keyboard Accessibility & Focus Management](/glossary/keyboard-accessibility.html) for a dialog example. [Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum.html)
- **Accessible authentication, 3.3.8 (AA):** If an authentication step asks users to do something like remember or transcribe information, provide an alternative or a mechanism that helps them complete it, unless another specified exception applies. Supporting password managers and paste can help users complete a password step. [Accessible Authentication (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html)

## An accessible form example

Consider a quote-request form with an email field. A persistent label is programmatically associated with the field. Keyboard users can reach it and see focus. If the address is incomplete, the form displays “Enter an email address in the format name@example.com” and programmatically associates that message with the field.

The error message explains the problem without relying on color alone. Previously entered values remain available, and the submission confirmation is perceivable with assistive technology. Test the full submission flow, including errors and confirmation.

See [Accessible Forms](/glossary/accessible-forms.html) for more on labeling fields, correcting errors, and checking submission feedback.

## How should teams test accessibility?

Combine automated checks with manual keyboard and screen reader testing. Check [text resizing and reflow](/glossary/zoom-text-resize-reflow.html) as users enlarge content. Include people with disabilities in usability research, and evaluate complete tasks as well as individual components. For a documented [web accessibility audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html), record the evaluation scope, evidence, and retest results.

## How do you make an AI interface accessible?

Use semantic headings, named controls, and a logical reading and focus order for generated content. A chat response containing a table or form needs the same accessible structure as other web content. Shared components help only when their configuration and surrounding task also work.

For streaming responses, test how content updates are announced. Avoid repeatedly announcing an entire growing answer or moving focus with every update. Provide a clear way to stop generation and return to the relevant content.

[WCAG status-message guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html) applies to qualifying updates such as waiting or completion messages; it does not make every generated paragraph a status message. Test the actual experience with keyboard and assistive technology, including interruptions and errors.

## How does web accessibility relate to AI browser agents?

WCAG addresses access for people with disabilities. Some AI browser agents also inspect the accessibility tree, where they can encounter the same field names, button roles, and control states used by assistive technology. [Semantic HTML](/glossary/semantic-html.html) provides the underlying structure, and [ARIA](/glossary/aria-accessible-rich-internet-applications.html) can describe states that a custom control needs to expose.

For the quote form, test whether a specific agent can find the email field, recover from an invalid address, and recognize a successful submission in a test environment. Record that result separately from human usability and WCAG conformance.

## Related terms

- [Semantic HTML](/glossary/semantic-html.html)
- [ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)](/glossary/aria-accessible-rich-internet-applications.html)
- [Component Architecture](/glossary/component-architecture.html)
- [Design System](/glossary/design-system.html)
- [Design System Governance](/glossary/design-system-governance.html)

sources: Read Me First, W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/read-me-first/)

contentMarkdown:
# ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)

WAI-ARIA is a W3C specification for exposing the roles, states, and properties of interface elements to assistive technology. It can describe information that native HTML alone does not express, such as whether a custom disclosure is expanded.

## What do ARIA roles, states, and properties do?

A role identifies what an element is, such as a dialog. A state describes a condition that can change, such as `aria-expanded`. A property describes an aspect or relationship, such as `aria-labelledby`, which points to the text that names an element.

Use native HTML when it provides the semantics and behavior you need. Adding `role="button"` to a `<div>` exposes a role. Keyboard focus and activation still need to be implemented.

## Example: A fare-rules disclosure

A native button labeled “Fare rules” reveals a hidden panel. While the panel is closed, the button has `aria-expanded="false"`. Activating it shows the panel and sets `aria-expanded="true"`. Closing it hides the panel and restores the false state. A native button gives you Enter and Space activation. Your code keeps the visible panel and reported state in sync. You can optionally use `aria-controls` to reference the panel’s ID.

## How do you test the result?

Verify that the button has the right name and state in the accessibility tree. Test it with a keyboard and a screen reader, and confirm that opening and closing the panel updates both the visible content and the exposed state. A Playwright ARIA snapshot can help catch changes in that exposed structure.

An AI browser agent that reads the accessibility tree can use the same role, name, and expanded state to find the button and decide whether to open it. Run the task with the intended agent to check whether it can open the panel and locate a specific rule. Keep that result separate from accessibility testing for people.
